prefill/prompt: Text is written in two phases. First, the prompt: here five tokens, all known before the model starts.
prefill/prefill: So the model runs all five in a single pass. The causal mask lets every position be computed side by side, and the pass stores each token's keys and values in the cache.
prefill/first: The same pass gives the probabilities at the last position. Sample from them, and out comes the first new token: mat. This phase is the prefill.
decode/one: After that, each new token depends on the one just before it, so each needs a pass of its own. Feed in mat, and one pass gives one token: and.
decode/cache: A decode pass holds one token. It reads the earlier keys and values from the cache, adds its own, and writes the next: it, then slept.
decode/count: Four new tokens took four passes: the prefill, which wrote the first, then three decode passes. A hundred new tokens take one prefill and ninety nine decode passes.
decode/wait: The prefill sets how long you wait for the first token. The decode passes set how fast the rest stream in.
decode/time: Put numbers on it. Say the prefill takes forty milliseconds, thousandths of a second, and each decode pass twenty five. A hundred new tokens need ninety nine decode passes: ninety nine times twenty five is two thousand four hundred seventy five milliseconds.
decode/total: Add the prefill: forty plus two thousand four hundred seventy five is two thousand five hundred fifteen milliseconds. Divide by a thousand for seconds: two point five one five.
memory/bytes: How long does a decode pass take? Memory is counted in bytes, and a model of eight billion parameters, stored at two bytes each, holds sixteen billion bytes of weights. A gigabyte, or GB, is a billion bytes: sixteen gigabytes, and every pass must read all of them.
memory/bw: A GPU reads its memory at about three thousand two hundred gigabytes per second. Sixteen gigabytes take five milliseconds, so two hundred tokens per second at best.
memory/math: The arithmetic is tiny by comparison: one multiply and one add per weight, sixteen billion operations, at a thousand trillion per second. Zero point zero one six milliseconds.
memory/bound: So decoding spends its time waiting on memory: tokens per second is the memory speed over the model's bytes. Faster arithmetic would barely help.
memory/pre: Prefill is different. Each weight it reads is used for every prompt token at once, so five hundred tokens share one read of the weights.
